title: Deconstructing My Lesson Observation Thought Processes
author: Sherrington, Tom
summary: Tom Sherrington reconstructs, at Oliver Caviglioli's request, the mental process he actually runs through while observing lessons as an instructional coach, distinguishing it clearly from a formal judgement or evaluation. He describes sitting with a student rather than circulating, taking private notes structured around "precise praise" and "probe" questions in the Bambrick-Santoyo coaching model, and watching for whether a lesson is currently in explaining/modelling, questioning, or independent-practice mode, since each mode raises a different set of diagnostic questions. He then sorts what he notices into three tiers of action, curriculum issues that belong with the wider team, individual issues that belong in one-to-one coaching, and collective issues that belong in team CPD, arguing that separating these three prevents unfairly pinning a team-level or resource-level problem on an individual teacher. A table maps each of the three lesson modes against the three action tiers, giving a compact grid of what to look for and where to route it. He closes by stressing that this is a "post-hoc organisation" of something much more organic in practice, and that he deliberately distils to a few key items rather than attempting comprehensive coverage of any single lesson.
points: Sherrington's core practical move is sitting beside a student rather than circulating, explicitly rejecting the idea that sampling more books produces "a more accurate/fair judgement," since he isn't there to judge at all.

His three-tier routing of issues, curriculum, individual, and collective, is designed to stop coaches from addressing team-level or resource-level problems as if they were one teacher's individual failing.

His "exemplar planning" note-taking habit, writing out the ideal answer to key questions in advance, mirrors advice he'd give teachers about planning modelling, applied reflexively to his own coaching practice.

He explicitly rejects the checklist framing of lesson observation, describing his mental model as a "post-hoc organisation" of an "organic and responsive thought-process," which shapes how the whole framework should be read.
quotes: I’m not there to judge or provide any kind of overall quality evaluation; I’m there to analyse learning problems as I see them and to support a process of finding solutions.

My goal is to get a feeling for what it is like to be in the lesson from one or two students’ perspective – I don’t like to wander about, causing a distraction. I’m not trying to kid myself that by sampling more students’ books I can make ‘a more accurate/fair judgement’ – because I’m not there to make a judgement.

Curriculum Issues: Very commonly, any given lesson throws up a range of curriculum questions. Teachers are typically using resources and a scheme of learning that is produced by their wider team, so it might be better to explore them at the team level, via the team leader.

I find it’s better to distil a few key items rather than attempt any kind of comprehensive review.. because any given lesson can’t support that; it’s the longer-term process overall from which a deeper understanding emerges.
It’s not a checklist I use in any formal sense; this is a post-hoc organisation of what is much more organic and responsive thought-process in any given lesson with some example lines of enquiry.
